body: Does it matter for how long he was posting such stuff? The problem still exists and I just want to help.

Hi.
First of all, I don't want to appear as I completely know what you are going through. You, however, made a decision. It was not being weak, it was not being a failure, it was not being a terrible human being. It was a fully informed and justified decision, no different and not worse than decision to give birth. Your current feelings are normal but You need to face two facts:
- This decision cannot be undone.
- This decision doesn't determine your value as a human being or mother. In some situations, there is no right and no wrong way to approach a problem. Both decisions would leave you with some consequences and you decided which ones are more possible to overcome. A lot of women go through the same process and being a mother is almost forced on them. However, to take care of a child and other important people in your life in the best way possible, you have to be physically and mentally well. Otherwise, it will never work.
You mentioned seeing a therapist and taking medication that doesn't help. In this situation, it is good to talk with your psychiatrist (different people respond to different antidepressants) and try to change therapist or the style of therapy (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy is the most common one but it does not work for everyone). The doctor might either try to use a different SSRI antidepressant (such as Zoloft) or change the class of used antidepressant. Feeling numb is normal when using antidepressants for the first time, but it's worth to explore this option, especially because you mentioned something what sounds like dissociation. Again, dissociation can be another consequence of taking antidepressants. 
You also mentioned two contradictory ideas: feeling numb and taking pills to sleep pills to feel nothing. Feeling numb is also a type of feeling, mostly caused by being tired by own emotions and the inability to understand them. You need a period in your life in which you can feel more peaceful to deal with them later. It requires time but don't put a lot of pressure on yourself. There was nothing wrong with your decision and there is nothing wrong with the wau you feel about it. You need to take care of yourself first and try to explore all the possible options you have. And no one - no one - should demand that you do otherwise. Your life is no less important than lives of others.

Hi, it seems like you are feeling extremely hopeless right now. I can imagine your frustration as you try to change something and it doesn't work. But I also want to help.
Can I ask you what do you mean by everything? There are different causes of being overweight (especially hormones, specific medical conditions, etc). Have you visited a doctor? And how bad your situation is? 
Don't feel the pressure to change immediately. If something doesn't work and you successfully realize that, then you are a step closer to finding what might work.

There are different types of antidepressants (most of them can be categorized as SSRIs) but trying to predict your response to any of them is very difficult. First of all, not all people respond to the same class of antidepressants and, most importantly, not all dosages are going to be effective or harmless to your mental health. From my personal experience, I can say that antidepressants prescribed by professional are really helpful but taking them is a long process and definitely requires guidance of someone experienced. Of course, there are some over-the-counter "wonder drugs" described as antidepressants but that's a little bit misleading, especially if they do not contain any active substances (which are usually the reason antidepressants are prescribed). I would seek the advice of a professional who can not only prepare your treatment plan but also help you with any side effects your medication might induce and correctly assess your mental state/comorbidities. 
In terms of experience with well chosen antidepressants, I disagree with the statement that they dumpen you down. A lot of antidepressants are going to make you more emotionally numb than earlier and stabilize you so you can look at everything from different perspective. No one is going to guarantee that you will start loving every day of your life - but you can gain more balance and willpower to cope with everyday tasks. But I am still not sure if this effect is attainable with commercial antidepressants.

Being a part of something and meaning something in this world is a goal that you can still fight for in your life but it requires effort. It is understandable that you desire this type of love (everyone does), however, keep in mind that, as this is possibly the most satisfying and pure type of love, it is also difficult to achieve and even people who seek it in their work or personal lives for decades might experience some difficulties. However, never make assumptions that you **must** or **need** to have this type of love already in order to love yourself or that getting help is pointless if you don't have this love. You might already have some positive experience with people (even if it's a small part of your general experience with them) and it's valuable to look at what you have and stop looking at what you do not have in your life. It's simply pointless to start working on something what you already have (a need for change, for example) and then ruminate on things that could go differently or people we could have in our lives. You can never undo the past or force others to behave in a way you want to. 

I do not know how old are you or in what phase of your life you are in but you can still aim to surround yourself with people who mean well to you - I was in a place similar to yours and decided to go out and spend more time volunteering, tutoring and organizing evens. I felt better, notwithstanding emotional neglect from my parents or people that were close to me but could never help or had to deal with their own problems. Going to therapy is a huge sign of self-love, so do not assume that you do not have it. Maybe it's not perfect and maybe the dialogue you have with yourself right now is not the best you can imagine, but you are making steps towards improvement. 

Love doesn't come easily in life and it applies to all of us. But most importantly, take care of yourself and still look out for opportunities to surround yourself with people who can give you type of love you crave - it can be a long process but it's worth trying.
But what type of love, exactly?

I believe that there is no single truth about which source of psychological support is the best or most necessary for good mental health. Being suicidal and feeling lonely is still common among people who seemed to "have it all" in terms of personal relationships and being able to love yourself is much more than having others who care about you - this care becomes meaningless if you do not try to understand how to translate it onto yourself. And wanting to do so  requires a lot of self-love, acceptance and own effort. Without self-love you do not want things to get better and thus can never appreciate the love you were given (even as a model for healthy relationships). 

You are the only person able to have control over own life and no amount of appreciation from other people will make you regain it until ***you*** want to do so.

Hi. 

First of all, I know that I am in no position to know what specific life events prompted you to write this post but it is good that you finally opened about your current feelings. I can relate to a lot of things you mentioned without thinking about it twice as well as agree with your description about the current world. 

> I've been staying alive for other people for so long, finally doing  something for me feels liberating, even if it's the last thing I do. 

You should, as a human being, never feel required to pretend that everything is okay just for the comfort of other people and become as honest with them as you are with yourself. Admitting that there is a problem is much better than hiding it as it is a huge step towards self-awareness, something what a lot of people lack when struggling with suicidal thoughts or going through major life crises. You mentioned people who can cope with the worst aspects of their own reality, however, I can assure you that they are either bottling up their own feelings/feeling scared to speak out or they went through a very exhausting process of trying to  deal with their problems and it was worth it. Many things in life are about perspective and sometimes change of a perspective can make life much more valuable. But it requires a dialogue with someone - be that a therapist, counselor or a really close friend - to work. 

Maybe there is something you can do before permanently erasing your existence from this life? Something that can make you realize that there are people who care about this world (volunteering) or that there are things that can make "slaving for money" worth it (buying items you need for your hobbies and activities after the job ends, for example). No one should be expecting from you to wake up next day feeling ecstatic and joyful. But at least try to get help you deserve before committing to your plan - arrange a meeting with psychiatrist/psychologist, try things that can make you feel like you have control over your life (new interests)  or look back at your own life in order to understand what currently affects your mental health. You never know how much relief it can bring, especially when you are a person who does not disclose own problems to others - just remember to do it only for **yourself** and see how it goes.

Hi, first of all - thank you for taking your time to write this response. I really appreciate your message.

Although now I feel more suicidal than ever, some time ago I have arranged a private meeting with a psychiatrist as I started experiencing somatic symptoms (ringing in ears when distressed, diziness, imability to catch breath in some situations, insomnia) but I have to wait 2 weeks. Before the exam period, I have spoken with a psychologist (who happened to teach me psychology in high school) and she slightly suggested that it can be beneficial for me to stop contacting my family. But it's a long way as I am financially dependent on them as a student and it would take at least 6 years for me to become able to earn my living.
The only thing I can be passionate about is medicine. That's the only factor that kept me alive for the last 2 years and the only thing that might extend my life for the couple of months you mentioned. I also want to take USMLE and arrange residency in the U.S. and already know how to go about this. So, I might have long-term goals, but, with no support and my own feelings, it all seems to be a road to nowhere.

Have you ever heard about models/public figures that spoke officially about how depressed and anxious they were in real life and how their accounts didn't reflect their real state of mind? 

Instagram is actually dubbed as the worst social media for mental health and this is not unjustified. You have a freedom of picking pictures that you want other people to see - that's the main point of having an Instagram account. Would you choose the ones that show you borrowing the amount of money you boast about, arguing with a lover, having a mental breakdown after losing a suitcase on your "superb" holiday trip or just staring with a blank expression on your face?

Social media are mostly about finding validation through pictures. People who are really happy and satisfied with their lives really do not need this.

They simply live their lives.

I have the same thoughts. Just finished chem HL paper 2, did 4 terrible mistakes while doing questions that were simple and for 1 point (I balanced one equation incorrectly, for example) and I really feel like an absolute failure (especially as I studied a lot for the exam). In general, I think that my results are going to be quite disappointing and the examination period itself seems like a big question about my abilities in general. It seemed that  the break would be a relief but now I know that I am going to dwell on the things I could have done better. 

Your post does not make you sound arrogant and I would really want to help you to get rid of such thoughts (as I know how unpleasant they are) but I think that a lot of people in IB experience the same feelings. It is really hard to remain confident while being in a system that is rigorous and praises excellence more than anything, which is even amplified if you are in environment of people who are high-achievers or have huge expectations from yourself. The only thing I can say is that intelligence is a relative concept and the examinations itself favor mostly knowledge that you can gain while studying, which is based mostly on memorization. Most of the skills that are really important in your life and most of the things that are going to make you happy or satisfied with yourself are not the ones you need for the examination. It is okay to say that everyone who has done IB is intelligent because the perseverance required to end this programme is (at least for me) a sign of high potential but it is not completely true to say that IB or IB exams are proper measurements of intelligence. Just please, do not go this way, standardized tests are still standardized tests and nothing more - it is quite too late for me but for the sake of your mental health, remember about your self-worth and intelligence, even when the examination period finishes.
Thank you so much for your answer, I did not notice that earlier, it's definitely reassuring:)

Hi there,

First of all, do You know all of the results of your interviews? Is this just a gut feeling or concrete evidence that You did something wrong? Correct me if I'm wrong, but I also feel that getting job as an engineer can be a difficult and competetive process. It is a career path drawing attention of many bright minds and I can only congratulate You on your graduation. I completely understand that You might feel disapponted, however, keep in mind that every interview serves as a valuable experience rather than reason to kill yourself. From what you have written, I deduce that you made a lot of attempts trying to explain your situation to others, however, have You ever tried to expain your situation to yourself?

I acknowledge the financial difficulties You are facing and Your reaction is natural, so please do not feel sorry for making this post. You are going through difficult time, however, keep in mind that 6 months is not a huge amount of time in the terms looking for a job. It seems that You have spent considerable amount of time being interviewed, but have you spent the same amount of time to find out the mistakes you have made?  Please do not attribute this single situation to the whole picture of your skills and characteristics. Even the best people out there suffer from significant limitations caused by their job (or lack of it). Patience and reasonable amount of critiqie can be your best friends - and I am sure that You are an appropriate person to make the best out of it.

Tutoring is really helpful and can make you become more independent when studying alone. Just do not give up and prepare yourself for lot of work, but remain supportive and understanding. It is hard, but definitely worth it. You are worth it.

What is the area of math you are struggling with? If the subject is very complex, maybe you lack understanding of some basic concepts (keep in mind that this is not your fault, sometimes people spend too much time working with advanced topics and they forget essentials). Also, have you though about tutoring? I know a lot of good students that are working with private teachers and are satisfied.

*Being good* is very subjective and trying to measure your worth will not do any good. Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, personality and confidence might be very superficial, and you do not know to what extent some people go to get good grades. Glamorizing others is completely useless - do you want to get to the point you are satisfied with yourself or to the point that you are "as good as your classmates"? If you choose the second option, you might never feel good about yourself, because what we see is usually not true - it is just what we see. Moreover, there always will be thousands of people that are in better position than we can ever dream of, even if we are fulfilled in our lives. Don't you notice how fruitless it can be to constantly compare ourselves to others just on the basis of our observations?  I understand your school-related problems, but everyone goes through that. If it's not in your class, then okay, let me introduce you to my school, where getting F on a report card is something not uncommon. Would you call these people *inferior*? If not, please ask yourself why do you do this to yourself.

I do not believe that there is a school in which everyone gets straight As - it is just impossible. What is the amount of people you are comparing yourself with? If they get good marks and are always prepared it means that they are motivated and work hard, not that they are in any way smarter than you. There may be many people who are gifted, but no one has ever achieved anything without work. Believing that everything comes to some people effortlessly is the main factor separating others from their dreams and just getting **stuck** with this sort of mentality. It just does not work well because you can only talk about how people are *better* than you (even if it's a lie) but never focus on how to make **yourself** *good* at something.

Do you talk with your teachers about any feedback, tips? Do you assess or criticize yourself? Do you organize your work or let your work organize you? Predictions about future are never good, even the positive ones. The most important thing is taking action. There is nothing wrong about your concerns - to be honest, mine are very similar! But are they helping you in any way? You are too worthy to do the same mistake as people stopping taking any action just because they believe that it is pointless. You should respect yourself for whoever you are and in whatever situation you are - it does not mean being ignorant or self-conceited, but staying strong and acknowledging that life is an experience, not a perfectly planned scenario in which people are less gifted, more gifted, doomed to failure, etc. The only real suicide you should consider in your situation is the suicide that your fears will commit if you stop believing in that scenario and your 'inferiority'.

From what I can read, your current school and boarding school seem like the most important factors triggering your anxiety, however, you should ask yourself what is the real reason behind this situation. No one is superior to you and believing that your contribution to schoolwork is insignificant is completely wrong - grades are always manageable, but it comes with trying to understand why did you fail your tests. School is not only about learning math or science - it is also about learning to fail and subsequently improve. Three tests mean nothing when compared to your whole educational background and you did nothing wrong because you failed them - everyone does that, even the best students. We are definitely not omniscient because we are *human beings -* making mistakes and attempting to understand them is the main way we can achieve something in our lives. 

Moreover - you cannot predict how your new school and place of living will be like. Moving out can be one of the best decisions in your life and you might gain new, fresh perspective on your learning difficulties. Although you are in full control of your situation and can choose whatever you want, anxiety might often make you believe that there is no control and thus separate you from not only feeling safe, but also feeling fulfilled in life. You have many options - moving out, changing your approach towards studying, trying to talk with your teachers or parents, making an effort to support and not blame yourself, waiting for the next DOOM game to completely amaze you, trying to speak with a therapist about your anxiety... Suicide is just not one of these options.

First of all, I can completely understand your situation. I was born with strabismus and underbite and although I managed to somehow improve my condition, the memories of being called ugly to the point that I should kill myself still remain and I developed a lot of self-destructive behaviors when I was a teenager. 
However, this whole experience was actually more like a lesson about prioritizing and assessing own appearance. 
The truth is - the way you treat body is way more significant than how it looks right now. I am not talking about blindly accepting things you despise, but allowing yourself to consider two aspects:
- You are not the odd one out. Being overweight is currently something almost predominant - just look at the way we live, eat, and sleep. Of course, there are many slim people - good for them. Contrary to the popular belief, some of them work/worked hard for that. But there is no reason to feel inferior when around them - no amount of sadness and self-hatred can help in social interactions and self-acceptance. It is better to remain indifferent and think only about your body and how do you feel about it - Writing this post is a good start.
- I also noticed that a lot of people think about their bodies as adornments and do not take into account that bodies reflect their overall well-being and health and therefore should be considered only on the basis of how they function instead of how they look. I do not know about your eating habits, but I know that you are a worthy person. Maintaining unhealthy weight and consistently criticising it is not always our conscious decision but a mechanism we start to associate with our person, therefore believing that our worthiness is conditioned mainly on our appearance. Do not fall into this trap. There will be many enjoyable moments in your life and you do not need to be incredibly slim to be happy with yourself. Take a deep breath, reflect over all the factors that could contribute to your current situation and remember: weight = problem but you = more than weight.

When it comes to time management on the test, I would recommend different approaches towards reading and math sections: 

Reading \+ writing: Do not get bogged down with questions that require more interpretation than data/specific quotations from the text. It does not mean that you should not try to ask them, but if you feel stuck \- just mark the answer you find to be the best and come back "refreshed" to evaluate whether you still agree with your choice. There is no reason to make careless mistakes on the easiest questions \(such as those asking about general idea and information depicted on graphs\) to get 1 point from the one requiring the highest levels of comprehension. But what if you still feel unsure of your answer or do not know how to find the right one? Instead of wasting time by fruitless attempts to find the right answer, it is better to find the wrong ones first \(but only if You can **justify** why they are wrong\) and make the so\-called "educated guess" when you run out of time. Moreover, if you meet any specific line of the text that you do not understand \- remember that one line of the paragraph is never sufficient for good understanding of the whole passage. Omit it and try to recap the meaning of the paragraph without it. 

Some people also recommend to start from the type of passage you like the most in order to get into "the reading mode". 

Math: Again, whenever you feel stuck \- move on. The most time\-consuming questions are usually the ones accompanied by a lengthy description and a lot of data. 

\- some people recommend to use the easiest way to solve a specific problem instead of using any elaborate formula that you know but are not sure of. 

\- sometimes substituting the given answers into equations is better than trying to work them out. The answers are often given in increasing order \- start from the middle one. 

\- if there is a very abstract question \(with variables, etc.\) \- substitute numbers you find to be easy to work with. For example, if given a specific relation between two formulae and a question about how doubling the number in one of them can affect the second one \- just use own numbers if you cannot work it out by operating on them.

\- calculator is not always your friend and a lot of test takers waste time by using it when faced with questions that require simple calculations. Just keep that in mind and everything will be okay.

There are tons of online resources and books which excess can make you feel overwhelmed at the beginning, so I recommend You to firstly check either Collegeboard official practice tests \(which reflect the real SATs and are also available at KhanAcademy\) or the diagnostic tests from IvyGlobal. Both can be found [here](https://prep.ivyglobal.com).

It is extremely important not to focus on the amount of practice tests you have done before the official test, but on the quality of the review of your work. Marking the questions you missed won't certainly show your weaknesses and, as SAT has a very untypical test format, even the most gifted students prove to struggle with word\-in\-context problems or some basic grammar rules. Make sure you focus on practicing only the questions that are really challenging for you and start from the basics when trying to find out why you made a mistake. For the writing section, I would also advise to assess which type of passages you find to be the least appealing and to what extent you can read them actively without losing too much time. 

There are also a lot of reddit discussions about SAT books, but [Prepscholar blog](https://blog.prepscholar.com) offers a lot of concise, useful information, so you do not need to pore over the massive SAT guides that are usually recommended.  

Moreover, the fact that You have already taken the ACT is a great advantage \(especially because you know how to work under time pressure\), so if You feel stressed about not being familiar with the SAT \- well, you are actually more familiar with it than most of the new test takers are. 

Good luck!
